item.title: Assessing fidelity-limiting factors and achieving single-qubit gate fidelity beyond 99.999% in driven silicon spin qubits
item.description:
Grade 0.735 · 3.5σ above the day's baseline · Kenta Takeda, Akito Noiri, Takashi Nakajima, Leon C. Camenzind, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Seigo Tarucha

Question. What factors limit single-qubit gate fidelity in driven silicon spin qubits, and how can fidelity beyond 99.999% be achieved?

Tools. Driven silicon spin qubits · Spin-locking coherence time ($T_{1\rho}$) measurement · Parity readout · Spectrally tailored pulse shaping · Microwave driving

Summary. The authors investigated fidelity-limiting factors in driven silicon spin qubits, finding that proximal reservoirs degrade spin-locking coherence and off-resonant excitation causes benchmarking artifacts. By mitigating these effects and using spectrally tailored pulse shaping, they achieved a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%.

Abstract. In semiconductor single-spin qubits, high-fidelity quantum gates have been demonstrated; however, achieving consistent performance remains challenging due to variations in driven qubit coherence, which is less explored than free-evolution coherence such as $T_2^*$. Here, we report single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.999%, achieved by dramatically extending the driven-spin coherence time and suppressing off-resonant driving effects that are detrimental to accurate fidelity benchmarking. We demonstrate that removing proximal reservoirs significantly enhances the spin-locking coherence time ($T_{1\rho}$), a critical metric for qubits under microwave driving. Furthermore, we reveal that in typical spin qubit setups using parity readout and rectangular pulses, off-resonant excitation of neighboring qubits causes substantial benchmarking artifacts. By optimizing device conditions to mitigate microwave-induced degradation and implementing spectrally tailored pulse shaping, we achieve a ${\pi}/2$ gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%, with remaining errors primarily limited by incoherent noise. These results showcase the mechanisms that bound fidelity benchmarking in state-of-the-art silicon spin qubits and provide practical guidelines for achieving and verifying high fidelities in these systems.

item.title: Real-Time FPGA-Based Multi-Parameter Feedback Stabilization of a Silicon Double Quantum Dot
item.description:
Grade 0.699 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · Johnathan Bryan, Tim J. Wilson, Hong-Wen Jiang

Question. How can a high-bandwidth feedback stabilization scheme be implemented for silicon double quantum dots to suppress low-frequency charge noise?

Tools. Silicon double quantum dot device · rf-reflectometry readout · Field-programmable gate array (FPGA) · OPX by Quantum Machines · Gradient-descent feedback (GDFB) approach

Summary. The authors extended a gradient-descent feedback approach in a silicon double quantum dot device using an FPGA (OPX) for digital signal processing and high-bandwidth rf-reflectometry readout, enabling continuous multi-parameter gradient calculation and quick gate voltage updates. This high-speed stabilization scheme achieved -6 dB noise suppression up to a bandwidth of 5 kHz, effectively suppressing low-frequency 1/f noise and maintaining device stability.

Abstract. Long term operation of semiconductor spin qubits requires active stabilization of quantum dot potentials against low-frequency charge noise. Previous work demonstrated a gradient-descent feedback (GDFB) approach on a silicon double quantum dot utilizing transport current measurements. We extend such a GDFB approach in a silicon double quantum dot device with high-bandwidth rf-reflectometry readout by utilizing a field-programmable gate array, the OPX by Quantum Machines, for digital signal processing. The OPX enables continuous multi-parameter gradient calculation and quick gate voltage updates, significantly increasing the effective feedback bandwidth compared to previous work. By operating with 8 steps per feedback cycle and an integration time of 25.6 $\mu$s, this high speed stabilization scheme achieves a -6 dB noise suppression up to a bandwidth of 5 kHz. This effectively suppresses low frequency 1/f noise, maintaining device stability over longer time periods, and potentially enables real-time control in large-scale quantum dot arrays.
